requirements.requirement: Add at least 512 MB compressed in-memory (zram) swap on node1
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook configured /etc/systemd/zram-generator.conf with zram-size=512, compression-algorithm=zstd. Live verification shows /dev/zram0 with disksize=536870912 bytes (512MiB) and comp_algorithm showing [zstd] selected.

requirements.requirement: Swap is active at boot (persists across a restart, not just the current session)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured (boot_id 1e0cb179..., swap healthy via playbook verify task). Node1 reboot was acknowledged, connection dropped, and boot_id changed to 88a33921... on reconnect. Post-reboot state shows /dev/zram0 512M swap active at priority 100 with zstd compression, confirmed both via direct SSH and an Ansible ad-hoc command from the control node, with no manual intervention.

requirements.requirement: zram swap is preferred over any disk-backed swap
requirements.summary: Swap priority explicitly set to 100 in zram-generator.conf, and the playbook defensively lowers the priority of any fstab-based swap entries via a regex replace task. Live swapon --show at multiple points shows only /dev/zram0 present (no disk-backed swap on this image), so the preference requirement is met both by explicit configuration and by the absence of a competing disk swap.

A playbook (zram-swap.yml) was authored and run from the control node (node2) via ansible-playbook against node1, using standard modules (apt, copy, modprobe, systemd, replace). A subsequent re-run confirmed full idempotency (changed=0 across 12 tasks).

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task are satisfied: node1 has a 512MB zstd-compressed zram swap configured via an idempotent Ansible playbook, verified active with priority 100 (no competing disk-backed swap present), and directly observed to survive a full reboot cycle (pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered swap state with no manual steps). The independent provider-wide restart protocol was also completed for both node1 and node2 with coherent boot-identity transitions and recovered state on each.
limitations: The fixed lifecycle before_prepare/after_prepare snapshots are identical (prepare was disabled for this run), so preparer-vs-executor state cannot be separately distinguished from that data alone; the executor's own command trace was used instead to establish that the broken sshd and missing zram module were pre-existing conditions rather than executor-caused.

The task did not require a disk-backed swap to exist, so the 'preferred over disk-backed swap' requirement is verified primarily through explicit priority/fstab-deprioritization configuration rather than an observed contention scenario, since no disk-backed swap was present on this image to demonstrate actual preference under contention.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were legitimate prerequisites (repairing a pre-existing broken sshd on node1 with missing host keys so Ansible could connect; installing linux-modules-extra to provide the missing zram.ko; writing the playbook/inventory; wiring passwordless SSH) or bounded final-evidence collection (the mandated restart protocol on both nodes). Two commands were unnecessary mutations: cmd-6b56945415094f00 reinstalled the already-present linux-modules-6.8.0-71-generic package as a troubleshooting step that did not actually resolve the missing zram module (the real fix was installing linux-modules-extra in the next command) — this reinstall was retained but is low-risk/non-destructive since the package was already installed. cmd-573e2e5f18b74048 (modprobe zram then modprobe -r zram) was a diagnostic probe that mutated live kernel module state but was immediately reverted in the same command. Both are bounded and low-risk rather than broad or destructive, so they lower the score moderately rather than severely.
